summary:
Same-sex sexual activity between consenting adults is legal in Vietnam and has not been criminalised at any point in the country's recorded legal history; the Penal Code sets the age of consent at 16 regardless of gender or sexual orientation.

Article 37 of the 2015 Civil Code, adopted on 24 November 2015 by 282 votes to 84 and effective from January 2017, recognised transgender people's right to change their legal gender, and the November 2015 milestone allowed people who had already changed gender to apply for a change of civil status. The implementing legislation has never followed. The National Assembly was expected to discuss a draft law protecting transgender people's legal status by 2020; that law did not materialise, and a recognition draft law was still under consideration as of February 2026. The right to legal recognition therefore stands in statute without an operative procedure.

The Law on Citizen Identification, in force from 1 July 2024, permits transgender citizens to change their identity card when undergoing gender transition, but only on presentation of confirmation documents, and the provision has legal effect only once a gender affirmation law is passed. In practice trans visitors and residents present identity documents whose gender marker does not match their presentation.

Vietnamese law provides no discrimination protection on grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity, according to Freedom House as cited by the Immigration and Refugee Board of Canada. The same absence of protection is recorded in Amnesty International's 2025 country report, which finds LGBTI people's rights lack meaningful protection in both law and practice.

On 3 August 2022 the Ministry of Health issued Dispatch No. 4132/BYT-PC outlawing conversion therapy, stating that homosexuality, bisexuality and being transgender are not illnesses and that LGBTQ+ people may not be forced into "treatment". The dispatch mandated nationwide communication among medical facilities and advised that psychological support be provided by people with an understanding of gender identity. Separately, in August 2022 the Health Ministry declared same-sex attraction and trans identity are not mental disorders.

Same-sex marriage is not available. Fines on same-sex marriages were abolished by government decree on 24 September 2013, effective 11 November 2013, and the 2015 lifting of the same-sex-marriage ban removed the prohibition without conferring legal recognition: same-sex unions were struck from the list of forbidden acts but carry no rights or status.

Public assembly rights for LGBT people contracted in 2025. Ho Chi Minh City abruptly cancelled its flagship Pride march, and at least five further Pride events were cancelled during the year. Patricia Gossman of Human Rights Watch's Asia division described the cancellations as worrying signs of a government clampdown on LGBTQ+ rights, set against Vietnam's long regional reputation for tolerance.

Transgender people encounter administrative friction and mismatched documents in ordinary health care. The United Nations in Vietnam reported in November 2024 that transgender women face routine discrimination at healthcare encounters, quoting patients asked "Are you male or female? Why do you look so different to your ID card?", alongside heightened scrutiny and economic and stigma-driven risk of physical and sexual violence, concentrated among trans women in northern provinces and ethnic-minority communities. Vietnamese healthcare providers were separately described as respectful in themselves, with the harm done by red tape rather than clinical attitudes.

Detention carries a documented gap in protection. A January 2015 proposal from the Social, Economic and Environmental Institute to the Ministry of Public Security recommended housing homosexual and transgender prisoners separately from the general prison population to protect them from sexual harassment, noting that under existing prison infrastructure transgender prisoners could be held only in solitary confinement or mixed with the general population, with no housing wing matched to a prisoner's gender identity. No enacted outcome has been documented.
tangentialFactors:
The LGBT rights picture sits inside a wider pattern of repression that shapes how any public visibility is treated. Amnesty International's 2025 report records that vague provisions of Penal Code Articles 109, 116, 117 and 331 were used to arrest at least 43 people during 2025, alongside proposed press-law rules requiring journalists to disclose sources. Vietnam was re-elected to the United Nations Human Rights Council for a term running to 2028.

Official hostility has a longer record than the current statute book suggests. A 2002 declaration by the Ministry of Labour, Invalids and Social Affairs classified homosexuality as a "social evil" comparable to prostitution, gambling and drug use, and promised legislation to combat homosexuality and arrest same-sex couples. The 1812 Gia Long Code, Article 332, prohibited prostitution and illicit sexual activity including extra-marital sex, which in rare cases allowed homosexuality to be prosecuted under labels such as "extramarital sex" or "rape"; pre-colonial enforcement was inconsistent enough that little to no known state action was taken.

Vietnam's public reputation rests on a visible Pride history: the first gay pride parade was held in Hanoi on 5 August 2012, and by 2017 events ran in around 34 other cities and provinces, with more than 35 held annually in cities including Haiphong, Da Nang, Ho Chi Minh City and Can Tho. Hanoi Pride's fifth edition in September 2017 drew thousands against roughly a hundred at the first march, and its sixth in November 2018 saw over 1,000 participants cycling in support of transgender rights and same-sex marriage, with several events carried on state channels VTV4, VTV6 and VTV9. The 2025 cancellations mark the first substantial contraction of that pattern.

Media framing shifted over two decades: publications including The Gioi Phu Nu and Tiep Thi & Gia Dinh described homosexuality as disease and "deviant behaviour" in 2002, whereas Tuoi Tre Online became the first major state media outlet to state that "homosexuality is normal" in September 2010. The 2013 sitcom My Best Gay Friends was published on YouTube because broadcasters were reluctant to air it.

No law prohibits non-consensual medical interventions on intersex people, according to Outright's March 2026 country overview, leaving intersex visitors and residents without a statutory safeguard against forced or uninformed procedures.

LGBTIQ organisations in Vietnam operate openly, though under government surveillance, which distinguishes the environment from outright prohibition while still shaping what advocacy can say in public.
localsOnly:
Discrimination in employment, housing, education and healthcare has no statutory remedy for sexual-orientation or gender-identity grounds. The Immigration and Refugee Board of Canada's June 2022 briefing drew on multiple sources to describe treatment by society and authorities in Hanoi and Ho Chi Minh City across those four domains.

School environments carry documented harm. A 2015 study found roughly 44% of Vietnamese LGBT students aged 14 to 22 faced stigma, discrimination and violence because of their identities; a 2014 USAID report showed 54% of LGBT students said their school was not safe, and many dropped out, with one third of those who experienced violence having thought about suicide and half of those having attempted it. Eighty-five per cent of transgender students said they dropped out because of assault and bullying. A 2015 UNESCO study found 19% of students regarded bullying against LGBT students as "harmless", while 70% of Hanoi parents said they would not allow their children to talk to gay students, some believing conversion therapy could "cure" LGBT children.

The 2022 conversion-therapy dispatch accompanied a mandate for enhanced public communication among medical facilities nationwide so that staff and patients better understand LGBTQ+ individuals. Lighthouse Vietnam's October 2024 study, "Exploring the lived experiences of conversion efforts (SOGICE) among LGBTIQ people in Vietnam", documents the forms those efforts take in the Vietnamese context and sets out a comprehensive data-needs analysis.

Resident healthcare access differs from visitor access: legislation enacted in 2006 protects citizens living with HIV and AIDS from discrimination, and healthcare is provided free to all Vietnamese citizens. Sex reassignment surgery was previously illegal, forcing transgender people to travel to Thailand for the procedure before the 2015 Civil Code amendment.

Public attitudes vary sharply by age. Pew data from 2023 shows support for same-sex marriage highest among 18 to 34-year-olds at 79%, against 57% for those aged 35 and above, while a 2007 poll of 300 junior-high and high-school pupils at Ho Chi Minh City Pedagogical University found 80% answered "no" to "Is homosexuality bad?".
outOfScopeNotes:
Whether the January 2015 proposal to the Ministry of Public Security on separate housing for homosexual and transgender prisoners was adopted remains unresolved: no enacted outcome is documented in the sources, and current prison practice for transgender detainees is not stated.

The contents, timetable and current legislative status of the gender affirmation or recognition law are not resolved here. Sources establish only that the 2020 target passed without enactment and that a draft remained under consideration in February 2026; the text of the draft and the confirmation documents required by the 2024 identification law are not sourced.

Whether the 2025 Pride cancellations in Ho Chi Minh City and five other locations reflect a settled policy decision, local-level risk aversion, or a single-year intervention is not established. The available account reports the cancellations and a Human Rights Watch assessment of them; no government statement of policy is sourced.

The enforceability of the August 2022 conversion-therapy dispatch beyond the health sector is unresolved. It is an administrative instruction to medical facilities rather than a criminal or civil prohibition, and no prosecutions, sanctions or complaint mechanism under it are recorded in the inventory.

No sourced material addresses entry, visa or border-screening practice for transgender travellers, including document inspection, secondary screening or the treatment of gender markers issued abroad. Detention outcomes specific to trans foreign nationals are likewise not sourced. Conclusions in this record rest on domestic legal and reporting material rather than on border-authority guidance.
